subtitle: Trace how Title VI, Section 504 and Section 1557 attach to a federally funded DSD program and its subrecipients, and build language access, program access and reasonable modification into a program's design before launch rather than after complaints.
audience: For DHS and DSD leaders, program and policy managers, and contract and grant managers who design or oversee federally funded programs that counties, lead agencies and providers carry out.

lessons.title: Who carries the duty: recipients, subrecipients and the chain of funding
objectives: Explain how federal civil rights duties attach to DHS and to the counties, lead agencies and providers that receive federal funds through it.
Identify the templates, contracts, rates and systems a state agency designs as methods of administration that can carry a barrier into every local office.
Describe how the three laws differ, including the 2026 change that limited HHS's Title VI regulations to intentional discrimination.
Map the chain of funding and oversight for one program you work on.
lessons.teaching:
Federal civil rights duties in human services usually travel with money. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal financial assistance. Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibits disability discrimination in the same kinds of programs, and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act applies protections based on race, color, national origin, sex, age and disability to covered health programs. When the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) funds DHS, and DHS passes part of that money to counties, lead agencies or providers, each organization that receives the assistance takes on duties of its own. The 2024 Section 1557 rule, for example, defines a recipient to include any state body or public or private organization that receives federal financial assistance directly or indirectly, which reaches organizations funded through DHS rather than by HHS itself.

Passing funds along does not pass the responsibility away. The HHS Section 504 regulation says a recipient may not discriminate directly or through contractual, licensing or other arrangements, and may not use criteria or methods of administration that have the effect of subjecting qualified people with disabilities to discrimination. For a state agency, methods of administration are the things leaders design: the eligibility screen a county must use, the notice template a lead agency mails, the rate structure, the data system a provider enters information into, the timelines written into a contract. If DHS builds a barrier into a template, every county that uses it reproduces the barrier. A subrecipient that adds a barrier of its own is responsible for it, and the state agency that funds and oversees the work still has to act on what it learns.

Advanced practice means reading the chain of responsibility before something goes wrong. For any program, a leader should be able to answer five questions. Which federal funds support it? Which laws attach to those funds? Which organizations receive the funds, and under what agreement? What does the agreement say about nondiscrimination, language access and disability access? How would DHS find out about a problem at the local level? Monitoring reviews, complaint routes, data reports, modification requests and conversations with county partners are all ways of finding out. A program that cannot answer the last question has no practical way to meet its duties, whatever its contracts say.

These laws do not work the same way, and they have been changing. HHS removed the provisions of its Title VI regulations that reached practices with discriminatory effects, effective July 24, 2026, stating that Title VI prohibits only intentional discrimination; the same rule says data on unequal outcomes can still help prove intent. The Section 504 regulation still reaches methods of administration with discriminatory effects. Parts of the 2024 Section 1557 rule have been vacated by a federal court, as lesson 4 explains. Because the requirements are shifting, this course teaches you to recognize civil rights questions and design for them, not to decide them. Whether a law applies to a particular DSD program, and whether a practice complies, are formal determinations for legal counsel, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and the person or area responsible for civil rights compliance at DHS.
lessons.keyPoint: Civil rights duties follow federal funds to counties, lead agencies and providers. A state agency stays responsible for the barriers it designs into templates, contracts, rates and systems, and for acting on what it learns from below.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is revising the intake packet that counties and lead agencies use for a DSD service funded partly with federal Medical Assistance dollars. The packet requires a signature in person at the county office. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, a county partner, mentions that their county quietly accepts signatures by mail for people who cannot travel, while a neighboring county turns those people away. A colleague tells {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} that civil rights compliance at intake is the counties' job, because county staff are the ones who meet the public.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} respond to the colleague's view?
choices: Agree that counties own compliance at intake, and send every county a reminder of the nondiscrimination terms in its agreement.
Treat the packet as a DHS method of administration, review its barriers before release, and ask counties how it works locally.
Let each county keep its own version of the signature step, since local flexibility already lets the willing counties fix it.
feedback: This is a reasonable instinct, and counties do carry their own duties. A reminder leaves the state's template unchanged, though, so the same barrier keeps arriving in every county office.
This places the design question where the design was made. It uses county experience as evidence and lets DHS fix the requirement once for everyone instead of relying on local workarounds.
Local flexibility helped in one county and failed in another. Leaving it there means access depends on where a person lives, and the state still owns the template that created the gap.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about a program you touch, or use the intake packet in the practice case. Which parts of it did DHS design, and which did counties or providers design? Where would a barrier in the DHS part show up, and who would be the first to notice it?
lessons.action: Choose one federally funded program you work on. Write down the funding source, the organizations that receive the funds, the agreement that governs each, and one way DHS would learn about an access problem at the local level. Bring any unanswered question to the person or area responsible for civil rights compliance.

check.question: Which of these is a state agency's method of administration that could carry a disability barrier into every county?
check.correct: A required notice template that counties must mail without changes.
wrong: A complaint that one person filed with a county about one interaction.
A county's decision to hire an additional intake worker.
check.feedback: A method of administration is a criterion, template, system or procedure the state sets for others to use. A single complaint is evidence about how something worked, and a county staffing decision is the county's own choice; neither is a state-designed method.

lessons.title: Language access under Title VI after the federal guidance changed
objectives: Describe what changed in federal language access direction in 2025 and 2026, and what did not.
Identify the language access provisions of the 2024 Section 1557 rule and Minnesota Statutes, section 15.441.
Decide at the design stage which documents are vital, which languages are needed and how people learn that free help exists.
Bring any proposal to reduce language services to the person or area responsible before acting.
lessons.teaching:
Title VI's prohibition on national origin discrimination has long been the federal basis for language access in federally funded programs. For many years, Executive Order 13166 and federal agency guidance built on Title VI told recipients how to give people with limited English proficiency meaningful access. That structure changed. Executive Order 14224, issued in 2025, designated English as the official language of the United States and revoked Executive Order 13166. The Department of Justice then rescinded its 2002 guidance to funding recipients, effective March 21, 2025. Its notice says recipients and subrecipients have a continuing obligation to comply with Title VI and that the denial of language assistance services can be evidence of discrimination under certain circumstances. HHS's 2026 change to its Title VI regulations, described in lesson 1, now frames those regulations as reaching intentional discrimination.

Other requirements did not go away with the guidance. The 2024 Section 1557 rule, as published in the Code of Federal Regulations, requires covered health programs to take reasonable steps to provide meaningful access to people with limited English proficiency, with language assistance that is free, accurate, timely and protective of privacy. It calls for qualified interpreters and translators, requires review by a qualified human translator of machine translation when the content is critical to rights or benefits or is complex, and restricts relying on an untrained adult who accompanies the person, or on a minor child, except in narrow emergency or documented circumstances. Minnesota law adds its own expectation. Minnesota Statutes, section 15.441, requires state agencies that directly serve the public and a substantial number of people who do not speak English to employ enough qualified bilingual staff or interpreters, and it gives translated notices about legal rights, duties or privileges the highest priority. Which of these apply to a given DSD program, and how DHS meets them, is a question for the person or area responsible for language access and civil rights.

For a program leader, the harder question is design. A program that arranges interpretation only after someone complains has already shifted the cost onto the person least able to bear it. The important decisions are made early. Which documents are vital because they affect rights, deadlines, eligibility or services? Which languages do the program's own data and its county and community partners show are needed? How does a person who cannot read the English notice learn that free help exists? What must a county or provider do, and what will DHS supply centrally? If DHS sends counties an English-only notice template and leaves translation to local budgets, the program has made a choice about who receives timely notice, whether or not anyone said so.

Changing federal guidance can tempt a team to scale back. Before doing so, separate three things: what a statute or binding rule still requires, what Minnesota law and DHS policy require, and what the program needs in order to work as intended. A notice that people cannot read does not inform them. Interpretation handled by a person's teenager does not produce reliable information or protect the family's privacy. Even where a federal floor has moved, the program's purpose, Minnesota law and the Section 1557 rule where it applies may still call for the same practice. Take any proposal to reduce language services to the person or area responsible before acting, not after a complaint arrives.
lessons.keyPoint: Federal language access guidance changed in 2025 and 2026, but Title VI, the Section 1557 rule where it applies and Minnesota law still bear on the question. Decide vital documents, languages and notice of free help at the design stage, with the person or area responsible.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is preparing a statewide notice telling people that their service authorization will be reviewed and that they must respond by a deadline. Counties will mail it. Several counties have told the team that they serve many people who read languages other than English. The translation budget is tight. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} has read that the federal language access executive order was revoked and suggests mailing the notice in English with one line saying people can call for help. {{SUPERVISOR}} has to decide what to recommend.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} recommend?
choices: Mail the English notice on schedule with the call-for-help line, and translate later if counties report confusion.
Ask each county to translate the notice locally into the languages it needs, using its own staff and funds.
Treat the notice as vital, ask the language access lead what applies, and plan translation before it goes.
feedback: A help line written in English does not reach the people who cannot read the notice, and a response deadline can pass before anyone reports confusion. The revoked order did not remove the other requirements that bear on this.

This sounds like shared responsibility, and counties may help. It also makes timely notice depend on each county's budget and leaves no check on translation quality for a document that affects rights.
This treats a deadline that affects services as vital, brings the legal question to the people who answer it, and puts translation into the schedule while there is still time to do it well.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a document your team sends that carries a deadline or affects someone's services, or use the notice in the practice case. If you could not read English, how would you learn what it says, and how long would that take?
lessons.action: List the documents your program sends that affect rights, deadlines, eligibility or services. For each, note which languages it is available in, how a reader learns that free language help exists, and who decides. Share the list with the person or area responsible for language access and ask what DHS currently requires.

check.question: After Executive Order 13166 was revoked and the Department of Justice rescinded its 2002 guidance, what is accurate?
check.correct: Title VI still applies to recipients, and other rules such as the Section 1557 rule and Minnesota law may still require language services.
wrong: Federally funded programs no longer have any obligation related to language access.
Each county may now decide on its own whether state notices need translation.
check.feedback: The revoked order and rescinded guidance were one part of the structure. Title VI remains a statute, the Department of Justice notice says denying language assistance can be evidence of discrimination in some circumstances, and the Section 1557 rule and Minnesota Statutes, section 15.441, carry their own requirements. Confirm what applies with the person or area responsible.

lessons.title: Section 504: program access, reasonable modification and the most integrated setting
objectives: Explain the program access, reasonable modification and integration duties in the HHS Section 504 regulation.
Recognize eligibility criteria and methods of administration that can screen out people with disabilities.
Use repeated modification requests as evidence that a default rule needs redesign.
Identify how planning, funding and service design can create a risk of unnecessary segregation.
lessons.teaching:
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibits excluding a qualified person with a disability from a federally funded program, denying them its benefits or otherwise discriminating against them solely on the basis of disability. HHS substantially revised its Section 504 regulation in 2024. The regulation spells out what the law means for recipients such as DHS and the organizations it funds. Three duties matter most for program design: program access, reasonable modification and integration. Each is a duty the program carries in its ordinary design, not a favor granted case by case. Parts of the 2024 regulation have been amended or had compliance dates moved since it was issued, so confirm the current version of any specific provision with the person or area responsible before relying on it.

Program access asks whether the program as a whole is usable by people with disabilities. The regulation prohibits eligibility criteria that screen out or tend to screen out people with disabilities unless the criteria are shown to be necessary. It also prohibits criteria or methods of administration that have the effect of subjecting qualified people with disabilities to discrimination. The same is true of methods that defeat or substantially impair the program's objectives for them. That effects language remains in the Section 504 regulation even though HHS removed similar language from its Title VI regulations. A required in-person orientation, a phone-only appeal line, an online portal that does not work with a screen reader, or a rule that forms must be completed without help can each work as a screen. Effective communication with people who have hearing, vision or speech disabilities is a related duty in the same regulation.

Reasonable modification asks whether a policy, practice or procedure should change when needed to avoid disability discrimination. The regulation requires reasonable modifications unless the recipient can show that the change would fundamentally alter the nature of the program. Two design points follow. First, a program needs a visible, workable way to ask for a modification, and staff at DHS, in counties and at providers who know what to do with a request. Second, a modification requested again and again is a signal that the default rule may itself be the barrier. Redesigning the default for everyone is often fairer and cheaper than approving the same exception one person at a time. Decisions about an individual request stay with the person or area responsible, such as the ADA coordinator or the program's designated reviewer.

Integration asks where and how services happen. The regulation requires recipients to administer programs in the most integrated setting appropriate to the needs of qualified people with disabilities. Its integration provision names planning, service system design, funding and service implementation practices that result in institutionalization or a serious risk of it. For DSD this principle is close to home; Minnesota's Olmstead Plan and the home and community-based services the division funds rest on it. A state agency can create a risk of unnecessary segregation through its own design choices, not only through individual placement decisions. A rate that pays more for a congregate setting than for comparable community support, or an authorization rule that is easier to meet in a facility than at home, deserves the same scrutiny as an inaccessible building.
lessons.keyPoint: Section 504 asks whether the whole program is usable, whether rules change when they must, and whether services happen in the most integrated appropriate setting. A state agency shapes all three through criteria, funding and system design.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{CASE_MANAGER}} tells {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} that people keep asking to complete a required annual reassessment by video or at home instead of at a county office. Counties have been approving the requests one at a time, and each approval takes weeks while services wait. The policy draft for next year keeps the office-visit rule and adds a new modification request form so that requests are handled consistently.
lessons.question: What is the strongest response to the draft?
choices: Test whether the office visit is needed, offer home or video to all, and keep a request route.
Keep the office rule, since the new form gives everyone the same clear way to ask for a modification.
Drop the reassessment for anyone who reports a disability, so that nobody has to wait for an approval.
feedback: This uses the pattern of requests as evidence about the default rule. It tests whether the office visit serves the program's goal, removes the barrier for everyone and keeps a route for needs no default anticipates.
A consistent form is an improvement over ad hoc approvals. It still leaves a possibly unnecessary barrier in place and puts the work of asking, and the wait, on the person every year.

This removes the delay but also removes a requirement that may serve a real purpose, and it ties treatment to disclosure. The question is whether the method of reassessment needs to change, not whether the reassessment should disappear.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of an exception your team grants often, or use the reassessment requests in the practice case. What does the frequency of that exception suggest about the rule it is an exception to?
lessons.action: Pick one rule in a program you work on and check it against three questions: Could it screen out people with disabilities? Is there a clear route to ask for a modification at every organization that carries it out? Does it make a less integrated setting easier to reach than a more integrated one? Note what you find and who owns the rule.

check.question: Under the HHS Section 504 regulation, when may a recipient decline a reasonable modification?
check.correct: When it can show that the modification would fundamentally alter the nature of the program.
wrong: Whenever the modification would cost more than the standard process.
When the person did not request the modification in writing on the program's form.
check.feedback: The regulation requires reasonable modifications unless the recipient shows a fundamental alteration. Added cost alone is not that showing, and the regulation does not make a particular form the only way a need can be raised. Individual decisions stay with the person or area responsible.

lessons.title: Section 1557 in health programs, and building compliance into design
objectives: Describe Section 1557's protected grounds and how the 2024 rule defines a covered health program or activity.
Explain what a federal court vacated in the 2024 rule and how HHS says it is enforcing the rest.
List the operating structures the 2024 rule requires of covered entities, such as a coordinator, written procedures, training and notices.
Plan a design-stage civil rights review with an owner, and use evidence after launch to revise the design.
lessons.teaching:
Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability in health programs or activities that receive federal financial assistance, among others. HHS's 2024 rule defines a health program or activity broadly. It includes any project to provide or administer health-related services, coverage or care, or to help people obtain them. It also includes all the operations of an entity principally engaged in that work, such as a state or local health agency. Because DSD administers services funded through Medical Assistance, many DSD programs sit close to this definition. Whether a particular DSD activity, or a county's or provider's activity, is covered is a legal question. Ask legal counsel or the person or area responsible for civil rights rather than assuming the answer either way.

The rule has been litigated, and the version HHS enforces is not identical to the published text. On October 22, 2025, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi entered a judgment in Tennessee v. Kennedy. It vacated the rule's provisions to the extent they expanded the definition of sex discrimination, which HHS describes as the rule's gender identity provisions. In a June 2026 notice, HHS said it will not investigate or enforce those vacated provisions and will continue to enforce the rule's protections based on race, color, national origin, age and disability, and the aspects of sex discrimination the order did not affect. The online Code of Federal Regulations may still display the original text, so read any provision together with HHS's current notices and with advice from legal counsel. Further changes are possible.

For covered entities, the 2024 rule turns civil rights into operating structure. As published, it requires a covered entity with 15 or more employees to designate a Section 1557 coordinator and to have grievance procedures. Covered entities must adopt written policies and procedures on nondiscrimination, language access, effective communication and reasonable modification, and train relevant employees on them. They must also give a notice of nondiscrimination and a notice that language assistance and auxiliary aids are available free of charge. That second notice goes out in English and in at least the 15 languages most commonly spoken by people with limited English proficiency in the state. Confirm with the person or area responsible which of these apply to your program and how DHS meets them.

The larger lesson of all three laws is that compliance built in at design costs less, and serves people better, than compliance assembled after a complaint. The decisions that matter are made when a program is designed. They include who is eligible and how they prove it, where and how people apply, and what notices say in which languages and formats. They also include what counties and providers must do and what data will show whether access is working. A design-stage civil rights review asks a short set of questions, records the answers and names who signs off. After launch, complaints, modification requests, interpreter use and differences in results are evidence about the design. A leader's job is to route that evidence to the people who can change the rule, with a date to look again.
lessons.keyPoint: The 2024 Section 1557 rule has been partly vacated, so confirm what is enforced now. Whatever the law at a given moment, a design-stage civil rights review with an owner, followed by evidence after launch, is cheaper and fairer than repair after complaints.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is two weeks from launching an online application for a new service funded through Medical Assistance. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} asks whether anyone has done a civil rights review. {{SUPERVISOR}} answers that the vendor certified the portal as accessible, the notices are ready in English and Spanish, and any problems will surface through the complaint line once people start applying.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} propose?
choices: Launch on schedule and track complaints closely for three months, then fix whatever problems they reveal.
Review notices, channels and modification routes now with the civil rights and language access leads.
Delay the launch until legal counsel issues a written opinion on whether Section 1557 covers the new service.
feedback: Watching complaints is worth doing, but complaints arrive late and come mostly from people who already found a way in. People who could not use the portal at all may never appear in that data.
This brings the right people in while the design can still change. It checks the parts a vendor certificate does not cover and sets up the evidence the team will need after launch.
Coverage is a fair question to ask, and counsel should answer it. Waiting for a formal opinion before any review, though, stalls work the team can do now under any answer.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a program launch you have seen, or use the online application in the practice case. When did anyone first ask a civil rights question about it, and what had already been decided by then?
lessons.action: Use the job aid to run a design-stage civil rights review on one program, notice or system change your team is planning. Record the answers, name who signs off, and set a date after launch to review complaints, modification requests, interpreter use and results.

check.question: What did the court's judgment in Tennessee v. Kennedy do to the 2024 Section 1557 rule, as HHS describes it?
check.correct: It vacated the provisions that expanded the definition of sex discrimination, and HHS continues to enforce the other protections.
wrong: It struck down the entire rule, so the coordinator, notice and language access provisions no longer exist.
It vacated the rule's protections based on disability and national origin.
check.feedback: HHS says the judgment voided the rule's provisions to the extent they expanded the definition of sex discrimination, and that it continues to enforce protections based on race, color, national origin, age and disability. Confirm the current status of any provision with legal counsel or the person or area responsible.

cards.back: An organization that receives federal financial assistance directly, such as DHS, or indirectly through another recipient, such as a county, lead agency or provider. Each carries its own civil rights duties.
A criterion, template, rate, system or procedure an agency sets for its own staff or for the organizations it funds. A barrier built into one reaches everyone who must use it.

HHS's Title VI regulations now reach intentional discrimination. Data on unequal outcomes can still help show intent, and Section 504's regulation still reaches methods of administration with discriminatory effects.

The Section 1557 rule's standard for people with limited English proficiency: free, accurate, timely language assistance from qualified interpreters and translators, with limits on relying on minors or untrained companions.
A document that affects rights, deadlines, eligibility or services. Decide at design which ones need translation and how people learn that free help exists.
A change to a policy, practice or procedure needed to avoid disability discrimination, required unless it would fundamentally alter the program. Repeated requests signal a default worth redesigning.
The Section 504 duty to administer programs in the most integrated setting appropriate to a person's needs. Planning, funding and service design can create a risk of unnecessary segregation.
A short, recorded review of eligibility, channels, notices, languages, formats, modification routes and data before launch, with a named owner and a date to look again.

aid.heading: Trace the chain of duty
items: Name the federal funds that support the program and the laws that attach to them.
List each organization that receives the funds and the agreement that governs it.
Identify the templates, rates, systems and timelines DHS sets for others to use.
Write down how DHS would learn about an access problem at the local level.

aid.heading: Plan language access before release
items: Mark each document that affects rights, deadlines, eligibility or services as vital.
Use program data and partner input to decide which languages are needed.
Say how a reader who cannot read English learns that free help exists.
Take any proposal to reduce language services to the person or area responsible first.

aid.heading: Check disability access in the design
items: Ask whether any criterion or method could screen out people with disabilities.
Make a modification route visible at every organization that carries out the program.
Treat repeated modification requests as evidence about the default rule.
Check whether rates or rules make a less integrated setting easier to reach.

aid.heading: Keep the record and the owner
items: Record the review's answers, the alternatives considered and who signed off.
Confirm current requirements, including Section 1557 status, with legal counsel or the person or area responsible.
Set a date after launch to review complaints, requests, interpreter use and results.

sources.title: United States Department of Health and Human Services — Rescinding Portions of the Department of Health and Human Services Title VI Regulations, Federal Register document 2026-15000 (effective July 24, 2026)
sources.note: Removes disparate-impact provisions from 45 CFR part 80, including section 80.3(b)(2), and states that data on disparate outcomes can still help prove intentional discrimination (lessons 1 and 2). It does not address Section 504 or Section 1557. Legal counsel assesses its effect on any program.

sources.title: United States Department of Justice — Notice of Rescission of Guidance to Federal Financial Assistance Recipients Regarding Title VI Prohibition Against National Origin Discrimination Affecting Limited English Proficient Persons (2025)
sources.note: Rescinds the 2002 Department of Justice language access guidance effective March 21, 2025, after Executive Order 14224 revoked Executive Order 13166, and states that recipients' Title VI obligations continue and that denying language assistance can be evidence of discrimination in some circumstances (lesson 2). It is Department of Justice guidance, not an HHS rule.

sources.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations — 45 CFR part 92, Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities
sources.note: Published text of the 2024 Section 1557 rule: definitions of recipient and health program or activity, the coordinator, policies, training and notice provisions, and meaningful access in section 92.201 (lessons 1, 2 and 4). The online text may not reflect the court's partial vacatur; read it with HHS's current notices.

sources.title: United States Department of Health and Human Services — HHS Informs Covered Entities of Partial Vacatur of 2024 ACA Nondiscrimination Final Rule; Core Protections Remain in Effect post Tennessee v. Kennedy
sources.note: HHS's June 2026 description of the October 22, 2025 judgment vacating the rule's provisions to the extent they expanded the definition of sex discrimination, and of the protections it continues to enforce (lesson 4). It does not itemize every remaining provision; confirm specifics with legal counsel.

sources.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations — 45 CFR 84.68, General prohibitions against discrimination (Section 504)
sources.note: Prohibitions that reach contractual and other arrangements, criteria or methods of administration with discriminatory effects, screening eligibility criteria, the reasonable modification duty and the most integrated setting (lessons 1 and 3). Checked as current in October 2026; other parts of the 2024 regulation have been amended or had dates moved.

sources.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations — 45 CFR 84.76, Integration (Section 504)
sources.note: Describes segregated settings and names planning, service system design, funding and service implementation practices that result in institutionalization or a serious risk of it (lesson 3). Applying it to a specific DSD rate or rule is a question for legal counsel.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 15.441 — Communications Services
sources.note: Requires state agencies that directly serve a substantial number of non-English-speaking people to employ enough qualified bilingual staff or interpreters, and gives translated notices about legal rights, duties or privileges the highest priority, within stated limits (lesson 2). It does not set DHS's current language access procedures.
